domains.title: Seonangshin, the Village Guardian
domains.subtitle: boundary spirit who protects settlements and travellers
domains.lead: Seonangshin is the village guardian spirit who protects settlements, boundaries, and travellers from harm in Korean tradition. The name means "Village spirit" and belongs to the domain "Village Guardian, Boundary." Seonangshin is the spirit who guards the village boundary, usually honoured at a shrine near the entrance to the settlement. The deity is believed to protect the community from epidemics, disasters, war, and wandering malevolent forces.

mythology.lead: The mythology of Seonangshin is preserved in Korean oral tradition, shamanic ritual texts, and classical sources such as the Samguk Yusa. The narratives are not merely stories; they encode social values, ritual obligations, and relationships between humans, nature, and the sacred. Some details vary by region and by shamanic lineage.

myths.title: The Shrine at the Village Gate
myths.text: Every traditional village had a seonangdang, a small shrine at the boundary where the village met the wilderness. Offerings of rice wine, cloth, and prayers were made there to keep disease and disaster outside the community.

myths.title: Guardian of the Threshold
myths.text: Seonangshin was imagined as a warrior or official who patrolled the margins of settlement. People passing through the boundary bowed or left a small offering to ensure safe travel and to avoid offending the guardian.

myths.title: The Dongje Festival
myths.text: Village communal rites (dongje) gathered the entire community at the seonangdang. The rite renewed the covenant between the village and its guardian, strengthening social solidarity and collective protection.

etymology.derivation: The Hanja 城隍神 means "city wall and moat spirit," the guardian deity of a fortified settlement. In Korean reading it becomes Seonghwangsin, but the folk pronunciation Seonangshin is widely used in village cults.

originalScriptNote: Korean names may be written in Hangul, the indigenous Korean alphabet, and sometimes in Hanja, the Sino-Korean character set. For Seonangshin, the Hangul form is 서낭신 and the Hanja form is 城隍神. Hangul ‘서낭신’ and Hanja ‘城隍神’ (Seonghwangsin in Sino-Korean reading); the figure is also called Dongbaek Seonang or Dodangsin in regional cults. The ASCII form seonangshin is a technological compromise; the capitalised restoration Seonangshin is the scholarly citation form.
syncretism: Seonangshin sits at the intersection of indigenous Korean village guardian cults and the Sino-Korean city-god tradition. Confucian reformers promoted official worship of local tutelary deities, while shamanic practice preserved the older spirit cults at village boundaries. The figure also overlaps with military hero cults: generals who defended a region were sometimes posthumously honoured as seonangshin. Today the seonangdang survives as a heritage site, and the rites are sometimes revived as community festivals rather than as explicit religious worship.
culturalLegacy: Seonangshin remains visible in Korean cultural landscapes: village guardian trees, stone cairns, jangseung posts, and restored seonangdang shrines appear in heritage villages such as Hahoe and Yangdong. The figure also informs Korean ideas of community, boundary, and collective responsibility. In a digital age, Seonangshin is sometimes invoked metaphorically to discuss online community safety and the guardianship of shared spaces.
extendedMeditation: Seonangshin invites reflection on the relationship between name, place, and identity. The restoration of the capitalised scholarly form is a small act of recognition: it marks the name as a proper noun of continuing significance in Korean culture and resists the flattening effect of ASCII-only domain names.
